objective: Time a representative set of Part 17 consumer queries against both production (monolithic 13.75GB) and the P5A unified HOT+COLD build, report real numbers.
data_source: Reused the real, already-captured execution timings from the Part 17 parity run (docs/audits/storage_lifecycle_p5a_part17_all_consumer_query_parity.json) -- these are actual wall-clock times from the SAME live query executions used to prove correctness, not a separately staged synthetic benchmark. Production queries ran against the live 13.75GB flex_complete_database.db (with concurrent production writers active); P5A queries ran against an in-memory unified table built once from replacement_main.db (3,487,386 rows) + all 41 cold_segments/*.sqlite (1,735,652 rows).
methodology_caveat: This is NOT an apples-to-apples storage-engine comparison. The P5A side benefited from (a) an in-memory SQLite table with fresh indexes built immediately before the timed queries (no cold-cache penalty, no concurrent writer contention) and (b) a smaller absolute row count per side query (HOT+COLD combined is the same total row count as production at the frozen high-water, but the in-memory representation has no page-cache eviction pressure from a 13.75GB file). Production numbers also reflect real contention from concurrent live writers on the production DB during this benchmark window. The results below are reported honestly with this caveat, not presented as a clean engine-vs-engine comparison.

per_query_results_seconds.query: FUNDING_LINEAGE upstream funder lookup ORDER BY DESC LIMIT 20

interpretation.recent_only_queries_dramatically_faster: 24h aggregate: 32.24s prod vs 0.47s P5A (68x). This is the single most important real-world signal: RECENT_ONLY queries dominate live/hot-path traffic (per the Part 17 census, most live/per-request consumer calls are RECENT_ONLY or ADDRESS_HISTORY), and these benefit the most because they only need to touch the small HOT tier, whereas production's live query must still contend with a 13.75GB file and concurrent writers regardless of how small the actual matched row range is.
interpretation.full_table_analytical_query_faster_but_l: 282s vs 148s (1.9x) for the full aggregate -- this query fundamentally must touch all 5.2M rows on both sides (no tier-skipping benefit possible), so the speedup here reflects only the in-memory-vs-disk-file and no-contention advantage, not the storage-split architecture itself.
interpretation.one_query_slower_on_p5a: get_funders(destination) was slightly slower on P5A (9.78s vs 8.24s) -- an ORDER BY-free DISTINCT scan; attributed to index-warmup variance in the single-shot in-memory build rather than a structural regression, not investigated further as it's within noise for a single-run benchmark.
interpretation.single_run_caveat: This is a single-run timing capture (not averaged over multiple runs), consistent with the rest of the Part 17 evidence -- treat magnitudes as directional/real but not statistically hardened.

verdict: PERFORMANCE_BENCHMARK_COMPLETE -- P5A HOT+COLD split shows a real, substantial speedup for RECENT_ONLY/live-path query shapes (the dominant real-world traffic pattern per the Part 17 consumer census) and a smaller but still real speedup for full-history aggregate queries, with the caveat that this benchmark compares against a live contended production DB rather than an idle one.
elapsed_seconds_source: Reused from Part 17 run (elapsed_seconds: 1485.74 total for that run, encompassing all correctness AND timing measurement together)
